Written for this course. Messages between three museum volunteers.

Priya, 08.14 — Been here since eight. Nothing in the hall yet. Banners still in boxes. Multicoloured ones for the courtyard, plain for inside — don’t mix them up.

Dan, 08.31 — On my way. Stuck on the ring road. Any sign of the bilingual signs? Ordered them in March, never came. Rang twice. No answer either time.

Priya, 08.33 — Arrived Friday. In the office, under the box of programmes. Sam’s doing the chairs — semicircle in front of the monoplane, not rows. Looks better and holds more.

Sam, 09.02 — Morning both. Chairs done. Two rooms interconnect now the builders have gone, so people can walk straight through instead of going back round. Much better for the tour.

Priya, 09.10 — Good. Programmes here too. Two hundred years of this place, and the first batch came back with the date wrong. Reprinting. Cost me an afternoon.

Sam, 09.14 — How many wrong? All of them, or just the first box?

Dan, 09.40 — Here at last. Parked behind the delivery bay. Illegal, I know. Ten minutes, no more.

Priya, 09.44 — Move it. Warden was round twice yesterday. Fined one of the caterers’ drivers. Forty pounds, apparently.

Dan, 10.31 — Catering confirmed. Sixty for the reception, forty for the talk. Tea urns from the church again. Ours still broken since March.

Priya, 10.36 — Fine. Guest book on the desk by the door, not by the monoplane. People stop to write and block the doorway.

Sam, 10.15 — Question. The figurehead — the semi-human one from the wreck — hall or side room? Was in the hall last time. Bit dark in there now, though.

Priya, 10.18 — Hall. Everyone photographs it. Side room’s for the biannual newsletter display and the old photographs. Lights fixed on Monday anyway.

steps.html:
Written for this course. The same thread later, a note pinned to a door, and an email.

Dan, 11.02 — Bad news. Speaker’s flight delayed. Intercontinental, so nothing before tomorrow evening now. Not tonight.

Sam, 11.05 — Which speaker? The semi-retired professor, or the one who pays for everything?

Dan, 11.07 — The professor. The multimillionaire’s driving up. Arrives Thursday, wants an hour in the hall first.

Priya, 11.12 — Fine. Professor first, donor second. Keep the professor short — lovely man, but speaks in a monotone and nobody lasts twenty minutes.

Priya, 11.31 — One more thing. Donor wants a photograph with the monoplane. Not with the sandwiches. Make sure somebody’s watching.

Sam, 11.20 — Ladder found. Behind the boiler, of course. Bulbs next.

Dan, 15.02 — Van driver rang back. Six banners still in the depot. Says Thursday morning. Chasing him again at eight.

Sam, 17.12 — Bulbs done, side room usable. Left the ladder by the stairs. Someone move it before Thursday, please.

Priya, 17.44 — Programmes reprinted, correct date, bicentenary logo on the cover. Two boxes in the office, one in the hall. Don’t open the hall box till Thursday morning, and keep it away from the caterers.

steps.title: Reading a word you have never met
steps.html:
Two things at once: how a prefix changes a word, and what informal writing leaves out.

A prefix carries its own meaning and does not change the word class. Legal and illegal are both adjectives; connect and interconnect are both verbs. If you know the prefix, you can read the word.

The quantity prefixes are the ones this lesson's wordlist is built on: bi- (two), mono- (one), multi- (many), semi- (half), inter- (between).

The negative prefixes are un-, in-, dis-, and mis-. In- changes shape to fit the sound after it: il- before l (illegal), im- before m or p (impossible), ir- before r (irresponsible).

Mis- is not simply negative. It means wrongly or badly: misunderstand is not the opposite of understand — it is understanding the wrong thing.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences. Cover the note and work each word out from the prefix.

The exhibition is bilingual throughout.
bi- = two languages.

Our biannual report appears in June and December.
Twice a year — not every two years.

The company celebrates its bicentenary next spring.
Two hundred years.

He wore a multicoloured scarf you could see from the road.
multi- = many.

The chairs stood in a semicircle.
semi- = half.

She is semi-retired and teaches two days a week.
Half retired.

Their systems interconnect automatically.
inter- = between one another.

It is illegal to fly a drone here.
il- before l.

The instructions were impossible to follow.
im- before p.

I completely misread the situation.
mis- = wrongly, not not.

steps.html:
1. You meet the word intercontinental for the first time.
  2. Take off the prefix: inter-. From the table, it means between.
  3. What is left is continental, from continent. So the word means between continents.
  4. Check the word class. Continental is an adjective, and a prefix does not change the class, so intercontinental is an adjective: an intercontinental flight.
  5. Now do the same with illegible: il- = not, legible = able to be read → impossible to read, adjective.

steps.modelHtml:
Norwood Rowing Club — 150 years, 6 September

The club's anniversary falls this year, and our biannual open day will mark it. Admission is free, and all signs and programmes are bilingual.

The centrepiece is the restored 1908 four, given to the club in 1991 by a multimillionaire former member. It has not been on the water since, and it will not be going on the water on Saturday either.

Two rooms reopen on the same day. The first traces how the river clubs came to interconnect in the 1890s. The second displays the multicoloured racing blades of every crew since 1912, along with the semi-human figure carved above the boathouse door, which nobody has ever been able to explain.

Chairs will be arranged in a semicircle for the afternoon talk at half past three. Swimming from the landing stage is illegal and will be reported.
